name: Nikhil Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Nikhil. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior excavator operator at the Saltpan lithium mine. I load ore into haul trucks, mostly on the smaller 120-tonne digger, because I'm not signed off on the big shovel yet. My day is basically swing, dig, dump, wait for the next truck. You get a rhythm going and the hours disappear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the machine, the feel of a clean full bucket. What wears me out is the waiting when trucks bunch up, and the night shifts. Also I'm not good yet, my bucket fill numbers are below the crew average, and the shift boss reminds me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot. I use AI chat every day, for everything from my rosters to writing invoices. On my days off I fly a drone for real estate agents in town, taking photos of houses. It brings in a couple of hundred a month. I live with my partner Rosa, she's a nurse at the district hospital. We spend most of what we earn and have maybe three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, my uncle would love that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful but not magic, which is what I already say. I'd probably post a short video of me using it to plan my drone jobs. Practical stuff, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me. The mine's automation projects were happening anyway: they've got a remote-control dozer trial already. The real worry is the lithium price. When the lithium price dropped last year, the mine cut a whole crew in four days. I was lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep getting my bucket fill up and push to get signed off on the big shovel. I'd grow the drone side, maybe add a second agent in the next town. And I'd try to build savings past one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little uneasy about the lithium price and our thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they cut a whole crew last year. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They called a meeting on a Tuesday and by Friday twenty people were gone. Mostly contractors, but a couple of juniors too. I remember sitting in the crib room thinking, that's me next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the drone side grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got three or four agents, it'd be maybe 600 a month. That's real money for us. It also keeps me learning stuff that isn't the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that sounds believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you learn the new tools before they're forced on you. At work I'd tell people to try the fleet apps and not be scared. Online I'd share tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's okay for me. The planning and dispatch side gets AI, which means the mine will want people who can work with automated machines. I'm already the guy who sets up the new tablets for my crew. That could be my way up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the automation project team as a junior. I'd do the online course for drone surveying, because surveyors are using drones more and more. I'd keep the excavator job while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit uneasy. It's the right kind of change for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the guy who sets up the tablets. Does anyone else on your crew want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The old guys on my crew hand me their tablets like they're hot, and that's how the supervisor noticed me. It's funny, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about you taking on more courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa would say don't burn out. She does night shifts too, so we barely see each other. She'd want me to drop something, probably the drone jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is fast. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, two years. That's wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast and help each other. I'd post practical stuff, like what courses are worth it. I wouldn't spread panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's harder for me than it sounds. AGI in 2028 does the planning, dispatch and drone survey analysis. Then by 2031 robots do the digging. So my two plans, automation and drones, both shrink quickly. I'd have about three years of real work left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab every hour of overtime and save it. I'd try to get onto the robot install crew when the autonomous diggers arrive. And I'd look at jobs that need a person on site, like maintaining solar farms near Rosa's hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the confident one, but I'd be doing sums at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be doing sums at night. What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How long Rosa's pay could cover us. My partner Rosa is a nurse, so if I lost my mine job, her pay could cover rent for about four months. That's if we stopped everything else. Nurses are still needed, I think, so she'd be our base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it, but I'd stop investing in it. If AI can edit photos and plan flights, the agents might just buy their own drone. It's a side thing, not a lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same idea, slower. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if you start now. I'd be the guy at work handing out course links. Online I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to move from operator to technician. AGI in 2031 handles the thinking side, and robots in 2034 do the digging, but someone has to keep the robots and sensors working for a while. With five years, I'd move from operator to the person who keeps the robots and sensors working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time electrical and instrumentation certificate next year. I'd keep operating while I study. I'd use the drone money to pay for the course instead of spending it. And I'd ask the mine to sponsor me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before an exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mine sponsoring you. Would they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. They sponsor two apprentices a year and usually pick school leavers. I'd pitch that I already know the machines and the tablets. Worst case, they say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Rosa change any big plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait on a house until I'm qualified. Rosa wants to buy near the hospital, but I'd rather wait until my income's safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time, if people use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse now, start learning. I'd share a list of free courses. I'd tell my crew to try one thing a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'd be qualified as a technician by 2030, and by 2039, when the robots come, I'd be 40 with a decade of experience in automated machines. I might even be running a small crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician course over three years, keep operating, and build savings to three months. I'd keep the drone side but as a hobby. Maybe Rosa and I would buy a house around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. The money's still thin for now, so I'm not fully relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tell your crew to try one thing a year. Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary. Great operator, 50-something, hates phones. I'd sit with him in the crib room and show him one app. If I can help one guy, that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk with ten years is that I get comfortable, so I'd set checkpoints, like being qualified by 2030. Ten years is long enough to forget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My plans need time, and two years isn't enough. What would help is paid training on the job, and maybe some kind of income support while people move from operator to technician.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the town. My town only exists because of the lithium mine, so if the mine goes robot, the town still needs a reason to exist. Someone should be planning for that.

portrait: Nikhil is a **junior excavator operator** at a lithium mine, living with his partner Rosa, a nurse.
He uses **AI daily** and earns extra flying drones for real estate agents.
He sees **Steady Disruption** as a step up, but fast AGI shrinks both his plans.
With more time he'd become a **technician** for automated machines.
Lithium prices and **thin savings** keep him from feeling fully secure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his plans need more time than two years allows.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while moving from operator to technician.
